raw_response:
I found seven useful references. The first five cover the runtime mechanism, compatibility constraints, and pod ownership pattern; nsenter is a narrower operational alternative, and the LXC example is explicitly later evidence.

1. Docker/Moby private-or-container PID namespace modes — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/moby/v17.12.0-ce/daemon/oci_linux.go
Useful part: Docker's separate private and join-container PID modes could implement an opt-in pod-wide sharing policy while preserving the private PID namespace used by existing images.
The opened implementation resolves a target container and uses its /proc/<PID>/ns/pid path, while the private branch requests a fresh PID namespace. An orchestrator could derive these choices from one pod option and give every application the same namespace target when enabled. Docker's own setting is container-scoped, and this code also joins the target user namespace when user namespaces are enabled. Date: pre-decision; the official release notes date this source version, 17.12.0-ce, to 2017-12-27: https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/17.12/. The current CLI explanation was also opened, but its live text is date-unknown: https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/.

2. OCI Runtime Specification v1.0.0 namespace path contract — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec/v1.0.0/config-linux.md
Useful part: OCI's namespace type-and-path contract could carry the pod's decision consistently to runtimes by selecting either a fresh PID namespace or one shared namespace path.
A PID namespace entry with a path joins that namespace; an entry without a path creates one; omitting that namespace type inherits the runtime's namespace. This distinction helps avoid accidentally turning the compatible private mode into host/runtime inheritance. The specification supplies the runtime representation, not pod lifecycle or public API policy. Date: pre-decision; the official notice dates Runtime Specification v1.0.0 to 2017-07-19: https://opencontainers.org/release-notices/v1-0-0/.

3. Linux PID namespace init and procfs semantics — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/man-pages-4.15/man7/pid_namespaces.7
Useful part: Linux's PID namespace rules could define the compatibility and lifecycle contract because PID 1 receives special signal treatment, its exit terminates the namespace, and procfs visibility depends on the mounting namespace.
One shared namespace cannot give every application its own PID 1. Images that require that identity therefore need the existing private mode. Shared-mode documentation should explain changed application PIDs, the namespace owner's lifecycle, and which process receives signals addressed to PID 1. The /proc mount must present the intended namespace's process view. Date: pre-decision; the opened versioned manual header is dated 2017-11-26.

4. rkt pod-scoped namespace owner and application launch architecture — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rkt/rkt/v1.29.0/Documentation/devel/architecture.md
Useful part: rkt's architecture could inform a pod-scoped namespace owner because its stage1 runs PID 1 for the pod and launches application processes underneath that shared execution environment.
This offers a concrete arrangement in which pod namespace ownership is separate from application entrypoints, while applications retain resource isolation. Its implementation uses systemd/nspawn and performs general init work, so only the ownership and launch arrangement belongs within this task's scope. Applications in that shared environment do not each remain PID 1. Date: unknown; versioned architecture and changelog headings were read, but the retrieved evidence did not establish a release date.

5. Linux setns PID namespace joining semantics — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/man-pages-4.15/man2/setns.2
Useful part: The setns contract could guide runtime startup ordering because joining a PID namespace changes the namespace of subsequently created children rather than the caller's existing PID identity.
The runtime must select the namespace before creating the application process and obey the documented descendant-namespace constraints. This is a launch mechanism, not a way to change the PID identity of an already-running application. Date: pre-decision; the opened manual header is dated 2017-09-15.

6. util-linux nsenter for selective namespace-aware operations — https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/nsenter.1.html
Useful part: nsenter could provide a diagnostic or administrative alternative for selected operations by starting a helper in an application's PID namespace while normal application containers retain private namespaces.
The helper-entry pattern can serve pods whose images still require private PID namespaces. It requires an authorized caller able to enter the target namespace, and it does not give all application containers mutual visibility. The utility forks by default when entering a PID namespace so the launched helper has the requested process view. Date: unknown; only the live manual was verified.

7. LXC 3.0 explicit namespace clone, keep, and share configuration — https://linuxcontainers.org/lxc/news/2018_03_27_21_15.html
Useful part: LXC's explicit namespace-sharing configuration could inform validation and compatibility messages by separating namespace creation from inheritance and warning that shared PID namespaces conflict with some init systems.
It supports referencing another process or container's namespace and requires sufficient privilege. Its container-level controls are implementation evidence; exposing multiple independently configurable sharing groups within a pod would exceed this problem's boundaries. Date: post-decision, 2018-03-27; this is later comparative evidence, not evidence of availability by the 2018-01-24 cutoff.

A design inference from these references is to retain private application PID namespaces unless one pod-wide sharing option is enabled, then have all applications join a single pod-owned namespace. The process responsible for that namespace must have a defined lifetime, and shared mode must make the loss of application PID 1 assumptions explicit. This inference does not require adding a general-purpose init system. Runtime joining, namespace visibility, and signal handling remain separate concerns that need clear behavior.

Search snippets exposed later Kubernetes process-sharing documentation, which I recorded and excluded without opening.
